title: Dissipation splits the Mott transition in one dimension
authors: Oscar Bouverot-Dupuis, Alberto Rosso, Laura Foini
abstract: Understanding how dissipation modifies quantum phase transitions is a central challenge in many-body physics. A paradigmatic example is the one-dimensional Mott transition, which in isolated systems separates a conducting Luttinger liquid (LL) from a Mott insulator (MI). Here, we study the fate of this transition in the presence of dissipative baths locally coupled to the density. Using bosonisation and an exact integration of the bath degrees of freedom, we show that dissipation fundamentally reshapes the phase diagram for bath exponents $s<3/2$, where $s$ characterises the low-energy bath spectrum. Rather than undergoing a direct LL-MI transition, the system develops an intermediate dissipative phase (DP) that is compressible and gapless, yet has zero superfluid stiffness. As a result, the conventional Mott transition splits into two distinct critical phenomena: a Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition from the LL to the DP, followed by a new commensurate-incommensurate transition from the DP to the MI. We derive an effective field theory for the latter transition and characterize its universality. For $1<s<3/2$, the critical exponents vary continuously with the bath exponent as $β=ν=1/z=s-1$, while for $s<1$ the transition is governed by $β=ν=1/z=0$ and the doping vanishes sharper than any power law. State-of-the-art Monte Carlo simulations quantitatively support our predictions. These results demonstrate that dissipation can qualitatively alter the nature of the Mott transition and generate novel critical behaviour in strongly correlated one-dimensional systems.
summary: The paper investigates the effect of local dissipation on the one-dimensional Mott transition in interacting fermions. It shows that for certain bath couplings ($s < 3/2$), the single transition splits into two distinct steps: a BKT transition to an intermediate Dissipative Phase (DP), followed by a new commensurate-incommensurate transition to the Mott Insulator. The analysis uses advanced field theory and RG techniques to characterize these novel critical behaviors.
main_problem: The central problem is understanding how coupling a quantum system undergoing a Mott transition to local dissipative baths modifies the nature of this phase transition.
main_result: Dissipation fundamentally reshapes the phase diagram, splitting the conventional Mott transition into two distinct critical phenomena: an LL-to-DP BKT transition followed by a DP-to-MI commensurate-incommensurate transition for bath exponents s < 3/2.
method: The authors employ bosonization to derive an effective field theory action, followed by Renormalization Group (RG) analysis and variational calculations on the resulting critical kink dynamics.
model_or_system: The model is a one-dimensional interacting fermionic system exhibiting a Mott transition between a Luttinger liquid (LL) and a Mott insulator (MI), with dissipation introduced via local coupling to harmonic oscillator baths characterized by an exponent s.
key_observables:
Compressibility ($\kappa$), Superfluid stiffness ($ho_s$), critical exponents ($ eta, 
u, z$), and the existence/nature of intermediate phases (DP).
important_parameters: Bath exponent $s$, which dictates the spectral density $J(\omega) \sim |\omega|^s$; the critical threshold $s_c = 3/2$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on bosonization, integrating out bath degrees of freedom exactly, and performing perturbative RG expansions around effective field theories for kink fluctuations.
figures_summary: Figures schematically illustrate the phase diagram showing the splitting of the transition (LL $	o$ DP $	o$ MI) based on $s$, and show finite-size scaling collapses confirming BKT universality at certain points.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical model and its effective action via bosonization, through RG analysis to determine phase boundaries and critical exponents for different regimes of $s$, culminating in detailed derivations for the two distinct transitions.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete example of how environmental coupling (dissipation) can qualitatively alter fundamental quantum many-body physics phenomena like Mott transitions, generating novel intermediate phases and critical behavior relevant to strongly correlated materials.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Schematic representation of the dissipative sys- tem. A one-dimensional fermionic chain (top), or equiv- alently an XXZ spin chain (bottom), is coupled to inde- pendent local baths characterized by the low-frequency spectral function J(ω) ≃α|ω|s.

Figure 2. Bosonized representation of density excita- tions. A particle added on top of the half-filled state ρ0 = 1/2 corresponds to a kink of amplitude −π in the bosonic field (top). The half-filled background also sup- ports elementary domain walls carrying half the particle charge, represented by kinks of amplitude ±π/2 (bot- tom).

Figure 3. Phase diagrams for s < 1 (top), 1 < s < 3/2 (middle) and s > 3/2 (bottom). The blue transition lines and the tip of the lobe belong to the BKT universality class. The magenta lines are second order commensurate- incommensurate transitions with exponents depending on the bath exponent s.

Figure 4. Typical field configurations ϕ(x, τ) on a lattice of size 256 × 256. The colourmap encodes the value of the field ϕ with darker blue signifying higher values of ϕ. Each kink has an amplitude π/2. We have highlighted one kink for each of the three rightmost plots. From left to right : a) is the MI with no kinks, b) is the DP for s = 1.25 with 6 kinks, c) is the LL with 6 kinks, d) is the LL with 20 kinks. The parameters are K = 0.35, u = 1, g = 0, α = 0.5 and s = 1.25 for a), b) and s = 1.75 for c), d). The data were obtained by working in the canonical ensemble (fixed number of kinks), so the chemical potential µ is not specified.

Figure 5. C/IC transitions at s = 1.25 (top) and s = 1.75 (bottom) for increasing L = β. Top: MI to DP transition. The MI is at µ < µc ≃0.8, while the DP is at µ > µc. Bottom: MI to LL transition. The MI is at µ < µc ≃0.5, while the LL is at µ > µc. From left to right: doping δρ, superfluid stiffness ρs, compressibility κ and renormalised Luttinger parameter KR. In all plots, only µ is varied and K = 0.35, u = 1, g = 0, α = 0.5. The black dashed lines correspond to the values δρLL, ρsLL, κLL, K of a pure LL (K = 0.35, u = 1, g = α = 0). The red dashed line in the lower right plot is at KLL−MI c = 1/4. Error bars are shown and often smaller than the marker size.
